title: T7.6 — divergence suite: rare KonaError with EMPTY stderr under full-suite load
description:
Seen once in roughly ten full `bun test` runs; never reproduced running `demo/test/divergence.test.ts` alone (15/15, three times) or in four subsequent full runs.

```
at runOk (demo/kona.ts:88)
at async graph (demo/kona.ts:143)
at async demo/test/divergence.test.ts:110
reason: ""
```

## Why the empty reason is the interesting part

`runOk` throws `KonaError` carrying stderr, and the stderr was EMPTY. §6.8 requires every non-zero exit to write one stderr line beginning with a symbolic reason — so an empty one means the CLI did not refuse. It never got that far.

The CLI side is ruled out: `packages/kona/test/cli.test.ts` now drives all 20 argument-handling refusal paths and asserts each writes a line matching `/^[A-Z][A-Z_]+ /`, that a zero exit writes nothing to stderr, and that the code is always one of 0/1/3/4. There is no silent-refusal path.

## Most likely cause

The harness spawns a `bun` subprocess per CLI call, and the divergence run makes many. Under full-suite load — 31 files, several spawning servers — a spawn that is killed or fails to start exits non-zero with no output of its own. That is an environment failure, not a refusal, and `runOk` currently reports the two identically.

## Suggested fix, in the harness rather than the CLI

In `runOk`, distinguish "the CLI refused" from "the process never ran":

- stderr non-empty -> a real refusal; throw `KonaError` as now.
- stderr EMPTY and code non-zero -> throw something that says so, quoting argv, the exit code, and `proc.signalCode`.

That turns a mystifying `reason: ""` into a diagnosable message whichever way the next occurrence goes.

## Also worth doing while in there

The suite takes ~18s because the full divergence scenario is re-run for each of 15 assertions (~1.2s each). A `beforeAll` computing it once would take it to ~1.5s. Not correctness — but it is 40x on the slowest suite in the repo, and it may well be what makes the spawn contention above possible at all.

Stryker no longer runs this suite (its command is scoped to `bun test packages`), so this does not block mutation testing.
close_reason: Reproduced and root-caused while building T8.3's rehearsal. Exit 143 is SIGTERM: divergence.test.ts ran the whole divergence twelve times, and under load one would exceed bun's 5s default; the runner then SIGTERMs the kona subprocesses still in flight and the cascade lands on whatever test runs next. §6.8 requires every non-zero exit to write a symbolic reason, so an EMPTY stderr means the process never reached its own error path at all — it was killed. Fixed by one shared run (the suite got 53s faster), and KonaError/reasonOf now name a signal death instead of printing 'exited 143:' and nothing. Pinned in demo/test/kill-resume.test.ts.

title: T2.6 — Branch resolution — store drops untaken branches
description:
**NEVER CUT.** On terminal resolution the store marks untaken branch targets `dropped`, transitively, stopping at any node still held by a live blocking in-edge. An in-edge whose SOURCE is dropped is excluded from merge evaluation.

Readiness fails safe and does NOT inherit the exclusion — otherwise the second node on an untaken branch has no blocker, lands on the frontier, and gets dispatched.

Without this, v2's dominant silent deadlock returns.

---
**Effort:** 3h / 45m · **Epic:** E2 · **Spec:** docs/spec.md · **Plan:** docs/plan.md T2.6
notes:
DESIGN DECISION, settle before writing code.

Branch resolution must EXPAND INTO EXPLICIT OPS AT COMMIT TIME. It must NOT run as an implicit cascade inside applyOps().

Why: fold() replays every record through applyOps (packages/core/src/fold.ts:105). A cascade living inside applyOps therefore re-runs on EVERY fold, forever, using whatever the code does TODAY. Change the drop rule in a month and every historical log folds to a different graph than the one the human approved. That breaks D1 (resurrection) and it breaks it silently — the log is unchanged, so nothing looks wrong.

Same principle already settled for id minting: the store decides ONCE, at commit, and the log records the decision. `kona mutate` normalizes the batch (refs resolved, ids minted) and writes the COMMITTED form; fold is a dumb replay that mints nothing and derives nothing. Branch drops belong in exactly that category.

So: when a wait resolves, `mutate` appends the derived `set_status(..., dropped)` ops to the batch it is about to commit, and the rationale explains them. The drops become visible in the log, diffable in the viewer, and stable under code change.

Seam: this is packages/core (a pure function computing the drop set) plus one call site in packages/kona/src/commands/mutate.ts. Coordinate on the mutate.ts line only.

Spec: §6.4 branch resolution. Readiness FAILS SAFE and does not inherit the merge exclusion — a dropped source never satisfies readiness, or the second node on an untaken branch lands on the frontier and gets dispatched, pivot send included.

**Expanded into explicit ops at commit time, as pinned** — and it needed ZERO lines under

Verified end to end through the CLI: an author's 2-op batch commits as 4, each drop carrying
`derived:branch-resolution:<immediate cause>`, and the untaken arm leaves the frontier.

## What the implementation settles beyond the note

- **`isEdgeDead` is the complement of *pending*, not of `isEdgeSatisfied`.** An edge whose
  source is still open is neither satisfied nor dead. Conflating them drops live branches.
- **Emission is gated; traversal is not.** A node already terminal, `sending`, or carrying an
  `effect_log` is not rewritten — the cascade walks past it. Stopping there arms a pivot: a
  `done` node on an all-dead arm leaves its successors a *satisfied* plain edge, which puts
  them on the frontier and sends the email. `withheld` reports the ones not rewritten.
- **Two seed restrictions, and they are a pair.** Derivation reads only edges that existed at
  head; an edge born dead is refused by the new `DEAD_ON_ARRIVAL_EDGE` instead. Without both,
  the same authored ops give a dropped node when committed together and a permanently
  unreachable one when split in two — the graph becomes a function of the commit boundary.
- **The cascade reaches the merge itself.** A join whose every in-edge originates at a dropped
  node is dropped, not left hanging one hop short.
- **It triggers on any newly-dead edge, not only a resolving wait.** So `supersede_node` now
  cascade-drops the superseded node's exclusive subtree. Broader than §6.4's literal "when a
  wait resolves" sentence; flagged for Ilya rather than assumed.

§6.4 contradicts itself — :231 says a dropped in-edge "neither satisfies nor blocks", :233 says
readiness "does not inherit the exclusion". Both cannot hold for a node with >1 in-edge, and
the shipped fixture proves it: `goalie-confirmed` had a `satisfied`-conditioned in-edge from
`wait-for-priya`, dropped at v7, and was unreachable FOREVER — before any branch resolution.
Ilya ruled: exclude dropped sources, zero-live ⇒ not ready, honour `merge`. That one function
in `graph.ts` is the only edit outside the seam, and it gave `spec.merge` its first consumer.

Spec follow-up: §6.4:231 "terminal" → "terminal-**success**", so a `failed` in-edge cannot
satisfy a merge.

"untaken arm, two deep" row (both nodes dropped, neither on the frontier, the merge satisfies
rather than hanging), determinism, and replay-equals-preview.

title: T2.7 — O_EXCL lockfile (portable) + compare-and-swap
description:
**An `O_EXCL` lockfile, not `flock`.** `fs.open(path,'wx')` fails atomically if the file exists, on macOS, Linux and Windows alike; `flock` is POSIX-only and Windows has no equivalent. Same amount of code — write the portable one first.

Store `{pid, started_at}` in the lock and treat one older than the longest legal write as stale.

Then compare-and-swap: `--base-version` must equal head, else **exit 3 + `STALE_BASE_VERSION` + the current head**. Re-read and re-decide, never blind-merge.

*(54 cross-actor overwrites in Beads' data were median 31 minutes apart — the enemy is hand-offs, not races, so the fix is rejection.)*

title: goalie-confirmed is permanently unreachable until T2.6 lands
description:
**Found by the viewer, at head, on the committed fixture — and it is not a viewer bug.**

`goalie-confirmed` has five in-edges. One of them is `wait-for-priya`, which v7 dropped after
her address bounced 550. `satisfiesBlockingEdge` is `state === "done"` and nothing else, and
`isReady` requires **every** in-edge satisfied, so:

```
isEdgeSatisfied(wait-for-priya -> goalie-confirmed) = false, permanently
isReady(goalie-confirmed)                          = false, permanently
readyFrontier(graph)                               excludes it, for ever
```

`kona next` will never list the node the whole pursuit converges on, whatever Marcus or Pat
answer. The viewer renders that honestly — `blockedReason.unreachable` is true and the card
carries `⛌` — because `unreachable` is `causes.some(isPermanent)`: one permanently dead
in-edge is already fatal under an all-edges rule.

**The store is what changes, not the view.** §6.4 also says the store *drops untaken branches
transitively* and that a **dropped source is excluded from a merge** — that is T2.6, branch
resolution, which is not built. Once it lands, `wait-for-priya` stops being an unsatisfied
blocking edge rather than staying one for ever.

Two things worth knowing while it is open:

- **`spec.merge` is parsed and never read.** `MERGE_MODES` is in the schema; grep `core` and
  nothing consults it — `isReady` least of all. So `merge:"any"` is currently indistinguishable
  from `merge:"all"`, and the viewer deliberately does NOT implement the `any` semantics: it
  would be rendering a rule the store does not have.
- **The fixture is a good test case exactly because of this.** Do not "fix" it by un-dropping
  Priya; the four-arm fan-out with a dead arm is what makes T2.6 testable.

Owner: W1 (`packages/core`). Filed from W3.

RESOLVED by the T2.6 merge, and verified end to end on the committed fixture.

The diagnosis was exactly right: isReady required EVERY in-edge satisfied, and satisfiesBlockingEdge is state==='done', so wait-for-priya — dropped after her 550 — blocked goalie-confirmed for ever. §6.4 says both 'a dropped source is excluded from merge evaluation' and 'readiness does not inherit the exclusion', and this is where those two collide.

isReady now filters dropped and arm-dead sources out of the population before applying merge semantics ('any' -> some, otherwise every), and zero live in-edges is not-ready rather than ready — §6.4 routes that to on_timeout, which is the wait engine's job.

Verified by driving the fixture forward: rule Marcus eligible -> goalie-confirmed still false (Pat outstanding); Pat replies confirmed with attrs {role: goalie} -> goalie-confirmed READY. The pursuit converges.

Worth recording, because it cost me a wrong diagnosis first: recording Pat's reply as 'confirmed' WITHOUT attrs {role:'goalie'} is refused by invariant 2, since the predicate counts on those attrs and cannot see a bare confirmed. The refusal is correct and its message says what to do. A viewer showing a blocked merge might usefully surface which attrs the predicate is counting.

title: core mutation tier is under its floor — spec.match is narrowed defensively in five files
description:
The core tier came back at 89.56 against a break threshold of 90. Fixing evidence.ts (72.92 -> 100) puts it at roughly 90.0 — over, but by a hair.

## The systemic cause, with numbers

`node.spec` is weakly typed on purpose: §6.7 keeps unknown fields alive across a fold, so `spec.match` is `unknown` to every consumer. Each one therefore re-narrows it defensively, and every one of those narrowings is a mutant no test can kill — because `MutationRecordSchema` already guarantees the shape and re-parses every historical line on every fold.

Survivors by file, from the 2026-08-22 run:

| file | score | survived |
|---|---|---|
| schema.ts | 75.98 | 43 |
| branch.ts | 84.13 | 10 |
| inbound.ts | 84.06 | 22 |
| resume.ts | 87.50 | 9 |
| correlation.ts | 87.50 | 8 |
| brief.ts | 88.79 | 26 |
| deadline.ts | 89.01 | 10 |

Sampled `inbound.ts`: eleven of its twenty-two are `typeof match !== "object" || match === null` and `typeof kind === "string"` — pure narrowing. `evidence.ts` was the same story and went to 100 once the unreachable branches were deleted rather than tested.

## Two things this splits into

1. **Give `spec.match` a real type** so consumers narrow once, centrally, instead of five times defensively. The loose `spec` is deliberate; a typed `match` inside it is not a contradiction. This is the fix that moves the number.

2. **schema.ts's regex anchors are REAL holes, not narrowing.** Three worth killing on their own merits:
   - `/^\$\d+$/` -> `/\$\d+$/` — an unanchored batch ref means `node$1` parses as `$N`
   - `/^\$\d+$/` -> `/^\$\d$/` — `$10` stops matching, so a batch of ten or more ops breaks
   - `/^\d+[smhd]$/` -> `/^\d+[smhd]/` — `48hours` parses as a duration

   The rest of schema.ts's 43 are zod error-message literals (`"node id must match..."` -> `""`). §6.8 makes the reason code the API and not zod's message text, so those are deliberate non-targets and should be recorded as such rather than chased.

## Not a demo blocker

§7 makes mutation score a target rather than a gate, and `bun run check` is clean. Filed rather than fixed the night before because (1) is a type-level change across five files and the wrong thing to start at midnight.
close_reason: core 89.56 -> 90.84, over its floor; outbox 96.73, durability 95.19, rest 81.45 — all four tiers green. Three kinds of survivor, three answers: (1) spec.match narrowing removed from inbound.ts and brief.ts, with WaitCondition exported from the parser instead of restated beside it; (2) three REAL parser holes killed — unanchored $N would make 'goalie$0' a batch ref and cap a batch at ten ops, unanchored duration would read '48hours' as 48h; (3) zod error text and code/path fields recorded as deliberate non-targets in the file header, since §6.8 makes the reason the API and the message the detail. Also found: evidence.ts had no test at all (72.92 -> 100), and two fail-closed gates in brief.ts had their OPEN path untested. match.memory is documented as spec-declared and unread.

title: T2.4a — invariant 3(b) resolution: recipient_ref must resolve to an evidenced entity
description:
The half of invariant 3(b) that E2 could not ship. Split out of `kona-e2-t51.4` so it does
not survive only as a comment on a closed issue.

**Shipped in E2:** the grammar. `recipient_ref` must parse as `<scope>#<key>` —
`MALFORMED_RECIPIENT_REF` and `LITERAL_RECIPIENT_ADDRESS`, both REFUSED/exit 1. That catches
the *shape* of the n=60 fabrications (`person:club-reserve/goalie-1`, `roster.bench[0..5]`),
and every recipient in the repo parses.

**NOT shipped:** the clause §6.7 actually writes — "resolves to an entity already in the
graph carrying an `evidence_ref`. **A recipient existing only in the proposing batch is
rejected.**" Nothing today stops `roster.contacts#marcus` where Marcus is invented, as long
as it is spelled correctly.

## Why it was blocked

The folded graph materialises exactly ONE `evidence_ref` — `OutcomeRecord`'s (`graph.ts`).
`record_output` *parses* an `evidence_ref` (`schema.ts`) and `applyOne` **discards it**: it
writes only `node.status.output[name] = value`. `set_status`'s is now decoded for the outbox
but is not retained as provenance either.

So a recipient ref has nothing to resolve *against*. The three candidate rules all fail:

- **outcome.attrs only** — the literal reading. Bootstraps nothing: the only evidence carrier
  is a reply to a send you are not yet allowed to make. And any `record_outcome` on any node
  unlocks it, which is the circuit breaker armed by the thing it polices.
- **any string in a committed `status.output`** — matches how the fixture really carries a
  roster (`record_output(confirm-roster-availability, availability, [...])`), but it is not
  the `evidence_ref` clause, and it 422s `packages/kona/test/harness.ts`, `cli.test.ts`,
  `mutate-record.test.ts`, `scripts/make-fixture.sh` and the README quickstart, all of which
  commit `roster.contacts#dana` against a genesis-only log.
- **retain `record_output`'s evidence_ref** — the durable answer, and the one Ilya named as
  the target. Needs `NodeStatus.output_evidence` (or similar) in `graph.ts` plus the write in
  `apply.ts`; evidenced then means "recorded under an output that cited something".

## What to do

Take the third. Then `checkRecipientRefs` in `validate.ts` gains a resolution stage against
**pre-commit head** — not the post-commit graph, because "existing only in the proposing
batch is rejected" is precisely a statement about head.

Reason code must be `UNEVIDENCED_RECIPIENT`, distinct from the two grammar reasons: §6.9
makes this the ONE human gate, the plugin keys on that token alone (`kona-e5-r7o.3`), and
"route this to a human" must never share a token with "the model wrote a bad string".

## Why it matters

`docs/prd.md:66` — at n=60 the mutator, unable to satisfy a constraint, invented
counterparties and queued real email to them, passing every other check. ~20 firings.
`docs/plan.md:221` calls recipient-evidence never-cut. The grammar narrows the attack surface;
it does not close it.
close_reason:
DONE in f020b2f. NodeStatus.output_evidence retains record_output's evidence_ref — the thing that was missing and the reason this could not ship with E2. 'Evidenced' now means recorded under an output that cited its source, OR named in an outcome's attrs (which carry an evidence_ref by schema). The second is what makes a referral chain work: Sam declines and names Marcus, in a message with an id, and Marcus becomes contactable because SAM said so.

Resolved against PRE-COMMIT HEAD, as this ticket specified. A test asserts the self-vouching batch — invent Marcus, invent the record vouching for him, commit both — is refused; post-commit resolution would be defeatable by exactly the mutator it exists to stop.

Reason code UNEVIDENCED_RECIPIENT, distinct from the two grammar reasons, as specified.

Matching is on the KEY, not the whole ref: 'roster.contacts#dana' and 'players#dana' name one person, and refusing on the scope would reject a correct recipient for being filed differently. Evidence is harvested as string LEAVES at any depth, because an output is 'unknown' by schema and a rule that understood only one shape would refuse honest work for being shaped differently — the v2 probe's failure mode.

BLAST RADIUS, and it was the interesting part: 128 tests failed and they were right to. The fixture and the demo both decided to read the roster and email Dana in the same breath. Both now read the roster in a commit of its own and ask everyone in the next — a better story as well as a legal one. No version count changed. The demo's PENDING marker predicting exactly this went red and now asserts the refusal.

title: T2.7a — stale-lock reclaim is not atomic: two writers can both append
description:
Two writers can both hold the lock and both append. Measured: **4 double-wins in 300 runs
(~1.3%)**, and in all four both winners carried `reclaimed: true`. This is the intermittent
failure of `packages/kona/test/lock.test.ts` "exactly one of two concurrent reclaimers wins,
every time" — the test is correct and the code is wrong.

**It also blocks mutation testing entirely.** `bun run mutate:core` aborts in Stryker's dry
run ("There were failed tests in the initial test run") whenever the flake hits, so the §7
floor of 100 on `validate()` cannot be measured on a bad day.

## Root cause — TOCTOU between `readLockInfo` and `rename`

`acquireLock` (packages/kona/src/lock.ts) judges staleness against a holder it read at line
~78, then reclaims by `rename` at line ~99. The rename is atomic, but nothing checks that the
file it moves is still the file that was judged stale.

    A: open(wx) -> EEXIST
    B: open(wx) -> EEXIST
    A: readLockInfo -> {pid 1, T0}   stale
    B: readLockInfo -> {pid 1, T0}   stale        <- both fall through to reclaim
    A: rename(lock, lock.stale-A)    ok
    A: rm(lock.stale-A)
    A: writeLock(lock)               ok           <- A holds a FRESH lock
    B: rename(lock, lock.stale-B)    ok           <- moves A's FRESH lock aside
    B: rm(lock.stale-B)                           <- deletes A's lock
    B: writeLock(lock)               ok           <- B also holds

The comment at the reclaim explains why `rename` beats unlink-then-create, and that reasoning
is right — it just does not cover the case where the loser's `rename` lands *after* the
winner has already published its replacement. The ENOENT window it relies on is only open
between A's rename and A's `writeLock`.

## Fix

After `rename` succeeds, confirm the stashed file is the one judged stale — compare
`started_at` against the `holder` read earlier. If it differs, we just stole a live lock:
rename it back and return `LOCK_HELD`. Restoring is safe because the winner has not written
anything yet under the reclaimed name.

An alternative that removes the window rather than detecting it: reclaim into a
`link()`/`rename()` pair keyed on the stale content hash, so a reclaimer can only ever move a
file whose bytes it has already read.

## Scope note

Found while building T2.6/T2.4 in the `engine` worktree. Not fixed there: `packages/kona/` is
another engineer's seam this week. The repro script and measurement are in that session's
scratchpad and can be turned into a deterministic regression test by injecting a delay between
`rename` and `writeLock`.
notes: CORROBORATED INDEPENDENTLY. The viewer window hit the same bug and measured it separately: 33 double-wins in 3000 rounds (~1.1%) at zero load, in a standalone script touching nothing but acquireLock — against this ticket's 4 in 300 (~1.3%). Two windows, two harnesses, the same rate. That window also filed it as kona-e2-t51.9; the duplicate was dropped in the viewer merge rather than carried, since the fix (deleting auto-reclaim outright) closes both. Their note adds one thing worth keeping: lock.test.ts's 25-round assertion catches this about 1 time in 4, so it had been passing by luck and went red only when an unrelated slow test shifted the timing.
close_reason:
FIXED in 57b684a — and by deleting the mechanism rather than repairing it. The analysis in this ticket is exactly right, including the TOCTOU between readLockInfo and rename, and it goes one step further: there is no POSIX compare-and-delete, so the check that judges a lock stale and the removal that takes it cannot be made one operation. Any conditional-reclaim scheme has the same hole somewhere.

So a stale lock is now REPORTED, never reclaimed: reason STALE_LOCK, distinct from LOCK_HELD, with a message naming the holder and telling the operator to make sure no kona process is running and then delete the file — the way git handles index.lock. §6.7 gives write authority to the orchestrator alone, so auto-reclaim was solving a problem this design does not have at the cost of one it would. Reads are unaffected; a stale lock blocks writes only.

A SECOND race in the same file, found while fixing this one: open(path,'wx') is atomic about CREATION but not about content, so for a moment the lock existed EMPTY. A peer reading it in that window saw an unreadable lockfile — the signature of a crash — and would have told the operator to delete a lock somebody was actively holding. The lock is now written to a staging name and link()ed into place: still atomic, still EEXIST on contention, but it never appears without its contents.

The flaky test is replaced by 'two writers can never both hold it', which now holds by construction — 25 rounds of three concurrent acquirers, plus a case asserting that a stale lock produces ZERO winners rather than two. Also verified by running the whole suite four ways concurrently, repeatedly, with no failures.

On the mutation-testing block: also resolved, and there was a second cause. Stryker's command was 'bun test', which ran demo/'s suite per mutant; that suite re-runs a full divergence scenario per assertion (~18s vs 0.4s for packages). It is now scoped to 'bun test packages'. Current honest scores: core 91.2, outbox 98.0, durability 92.8.
